Penalties for regularized and bias reduced estimation

Source: R/penalty.R
penalty.Rd

Builds a penalty on regression coefficients for the "ml" engine. The estimate maximizes loglik(beta) - P(beta).

Usage

penalty(
  type = c("ridge", "lasso", "elastic_net", "adaptive_lasso", "group_lasso", "scad",
    "mcp", "firth", "jeffreys", "flic", "flac", "log_f", "cauchy"),
  lambda = 1,
  alpha = NULL,
  pars = NULL,
  standardize = TRUE,
  gamma = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  groups = NULL,
  m = 1,
  scale = 2.5
)

Arguments

type

Penalty type, see Details.

lambda

Non-negative penalty weight.

alpha

Elastic net mixing weight in [0, 1].

pars

Parameters whose coefficients are penalized (default all).

standardize

Scale each penalized column by its standard deviation before penalizing (shrinkage penalties only).

gamma

Adaptive lasso exponent, or the concavity of "scad" (default 3.7) and "mcp" (default 3).

weights

Optional adaptive lasso weights.

groups

Optional group labels for "group_lasso".

m

Degrees of freedom of the log F prior.

scale

Scale of the Cauchy prior.

Value

An object of class regcomp_penalty.

Details

Smooth penalties (work with random effects):

  • "ridge": P = lambda / 2 * sum(beta^2).

  • "firth" (alias "jeffreys"): P = -1/2 log det I(beta), Firth's (1993) penalized likelihood, equivalent to a Jeffreys invariant prior. For canonical links of exponential families (logistic, Poisson log linear) it removes the first order bias of the maximum likelihood estimator and gives finite estimates under separation. I(beta) is the expected information for families whose eta second derivatives do not depend on the response and the observed information otherwise (documented approximation).

  • "flic": Firth estimates with the intercept of each penalized predictor re estimated by maximum likelihood with the other terms as an offset, so average predicted probabilities equal observed proportions (Puhr et al. 2017).

  • "flac": Firth's logistic regression with added covariate: maximum likelihood on data augmented by pseudo observations weighted by half the Firth hat values (Puhr et al. 2017). Binary and binomial families only.

  • "log_f": log F(m, m) prior penalty P = -sum(m/2 beta - m log(1 + exp(beta))) (Greenland and Mansournia 2015).

  • "cauchy": independent Cauchy priors with scale scale, P = sum log(1 + (beta / scale)^2) (Gelman et al. 2008).

Non smooth penalties (fitted by accelerated proximal gradient descent, FISTA, for models without random effects):

  • "lasso": lambda * sum(|beta|).

  • "elastic_net": lambda * (alpha * sum(|beta|) + (1 - alpha) / 2 * sum(beta^2)).

  • "adaptive_lasso": lambda * sum(w_j |beta_j|), w_j = 1 / |b_j|^gamma from an initial maximum likelihood (or ridge) fit, or user weights.

  • "group_lasso": lambda * sum_g sqrt(p_g) ||beta_g||_2 for groups (a vector naming the group of each penalized coefficient; by default the columns generated by one model term form a group).

  • "scad" and "mcp": folded concave penalties (Fan and Li 2001; Zhang 2010) fitted by the local linear approximation (Zou and Li 2008), a few reweighted lasso steps started from the lasso.

lambda is on the scale of the summed log likelihood: lambda = n * lambda_glmnet reproduces glmnet and ncvreg, whose losses are averaged over observations. The SCAD and MCP thresholds act on lambda / n.

Intercepts are never penalized except by "firth", which acts on the whole information matrix. Penalized estimates are not maximum likelihood estimates. For "firth", "log_f" and "cauchy" the inverse penalized Hessian is reported as the covariance and is the usual large sample approximation; for the others it is not a valid frequentist covariance and p values are suppressed. Choose lambda by cross validation.

References

Firth (1993), Bias reduction of maximum likelihood estimates. Biometrika, 80, 27-38. Heinze and Schemper (2002), A solution to the problem of separation in logistic regression. Statistics in Medicine, 21, 2409-2419. Puhr, Heinze, Nold, Lusa and Geroldinger (2017), Firth's logistic regression with rare events. Statistics in Medicine, 36, 2302-2317. Greenland and Mansournia (2015), Penalization, bias reduction, and default priors in logistic and related categorical and survival regressions. Statistics in Medicine, 34, 3133-3143. Gelman, Jakulin, Pittau and Su (2008), A weakly informative default prior distribution for logistic and other regression models. Annals of Applied Statistics, 2, 1360-1383. Tibshirani (1996); Zou and Hastie (2005); Zou (2006); Yuan and Lin (2006); Fan and Li (2001); Zhang (2010); Zou and Li (2008).

Examples

# Complete separation: maximum likelihood diverges, Firth stays finite.
d <- data.frame(x = c(-2, -1, -0.5, 0.5, 1, 2), y = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1))
fit <- regcomp(y ~ x, family = "bernoulli", data = d, penalty = penalty("firth"))
coef(fit)
#> prob:(Intercept)           prob:x 
#>     5.499443e-05     1.583693e+00 
set.seed(2)
X <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 8), 200)
d2 <- data.frame(X, y = rpois(200, exp(0.5 + X[, 1] - 0.5 * X[, 2])))
fit2 <- regcomp(y ~ ., family = "poisson", data = d2,
                penalty = penalty("lasso", lambda = 5))
round(coef(fit2), 3)
#> lambda:(Intercept)          lambda:X1          lambda:X2          lambda:X3 
#>              0.488              0.984             -0.484              0.033 
#>          lambda:X4          lambda:X5          lambda:X6          lambda:X7 
#>              0.016              0.029              0.000              0.000 
#>          lambda:X8 
#>              0.119
